You may doubt that, why not just using {1} or {2} to build a JSON?
There are various reasons:
{1} must output a well-formed JSON. If there is incorrect event sequence (e.g. {2} just after {3}), it generates assertion fail in debug mode.
{1} can handle string escaping (e.g. converting code point {2} to {3}) and Unicode transcoding.
{1} handles number output consistently.
{1} implements the event handler concept. It can be used to handle events from {2}, {3} or other event publisher.
{1} can be optimized for different platforms.
Anyway, using {1} API is even simpler than generating a JSON by ad hoc methods.

Completeness and Reset

A {1} can only output a single JSON, which can be any JSON type at the root. Once the singular event for root (e.g. {2}), or the last matching {3} or {4} event, is handled, the output JSON is well-formed and complete. User can detect this state by calling {5}.

When a JSON is complete, the {1} cannot accept any new events. Otherwise the output will be invalid (i.e. having more than one root). To reuse the {2} object, user can call {3} to reset all internal states of the {4} with a new output stream.
